pages.title: Collecting association norms
pages.c: **Association norms** summarize the words that people produce in response to a cue. A participant sees a word briefly and writes the first few words that come to mind. Collecting responses across people reveals which associations recur and which responses are unusual.
support: The task asks for immediate associations rather than a dictionary definition. Its outcome is a pattern of responses to each cue, so the same word can elicit several different associates across participants.
pages.d: An association is measured through a response. Presenting the same cue to multiple people makes it possible to compare their responses and identify common connections between words.

pages.title: LION · Association cue
pages.c: LION is an association cue. The task is to produce the first words that it brings to mind, allowing the responses to reveal connections in the participant’s lexical knowledge.
pages.d: A response such as TIGER would connect two animal concepts. It is a possible associate rather than a response that every participant must give.
pages.visual: The printed cue is LION. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: TRIPE · Association cue
pages.c: TRIPE is an association cue whose form resembles STRIPES. The shared sequence of letters does not establish a shared meaning. Similarity in a word’s form and a connection between its meanings are different relationships.
pages.d: The comparison between TRIPE and STRIPES makes the arbitrariness of form–meaning mappings concrete. Overlapping letters can occur in words with very different meanings.
pages.visual: The printed cue is TRIPE. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: FREE · Association cue
pages.c: FREE serves as a cue in the association task. A participant supplies words that come to mind from this cue, rather than choosing from a list of answers.
pages.d: The response is generated by the participant. Recording that response makes an internal association available for comparison across people.
pages.visual: The printed cue is FREE. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: STRIPES · Association cue
pages.c: STRIPES is a cue that names a visual property. An association can connect a property with an object or animal that has it, so associated words do not have to name the same kind of thing.
pages.d: STRIPES and TIGER can be associated even though one names a pattern and the other names an animal. This differs from the similarity between two animal concepts.
pages.visual: The printed cue is STRIPES. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: PEAR · Association cue
pages.c: PEAR is an association cue. Its form overlaps with BEAR even though the two words have different meanings. The resemblance between their forms does not turn the fruit and the animal into the same concept.
pages.d: PEAR and BEAR separate a formal relationship from a semantic one. A shared sound or spelling pattern is not itself evidence of similar meanings.
pages.visual: The printed cue is PEAR. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: BEAR · Association cue
pages.c: BEAR provides another cue for a freely generated association. Its overlap in form with PEAR illustrates that words can resemble one another without resembling one another in meaning.
pages.d: Association norms record the responses people actually give. They do not require the experimenter to decide in advance whether a response will be based on form or meaning.
pages.visual: The printed cue is BEAR. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: TREE · Association cue
pages.c: TREE is presented as a cue for the association task. The participant’s first responses provide evidence about which words are readily connected with it in that task context.
pages.d: A cue remains the same physical word while different people can supply different associates. The norm summarizes those responses rather than treating one response as the word’s only association.
pages.visual: The printed cue is TREE. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: TIGER · Association cue
pages.c: TIGER can be connected with LION through their similar meanings as animals and with STRIPES through a characteristic pattern. These relationships illustrate why association and similarity are not interchangeable.
pages.d: An animal can be associated with one of its properties. Two animal names can also be related through shared category membership. Both can contribute to the structure of a lexical network.
pages.visual: The printed cue is TIGER. Its role is to elicit the participant’s own response, rather than to supply a completed association norm.

pages.title: Association and the arbitrariness of word form
pages.c: **LION, TIGER and STRIPES** illustrate different kinds of connection between meanings. LION and TIGER name similar animals, while TIGER and STRIPES connect an animal with a characteristic property. Their associations can be measured by counting how often participants supply one in response to another.
support: TRIPE and STRIPES, and PEAR and BEAR, make a different point. Their forms overlap, but similar form does not guarantee similar meaning. The relationship between the sound or spelling of a word and its meaning is largely arbitrary.
pages.d: To describe a lexical relationship precisely, distinguish similarity of form, similarity of meaning and a tendency for one word to bring another to mind. These can overlap, but none is a substitute for measuring the others.
pages.visual: The three cues LION, TIGER and STRIPES provide the conceptual links for an association network. The paired words TRIPE/STRIPES and PEAR/BEAR illustrate form overlap without a matching semantic relationship.

pages.title: Association norms depend on the task context
pages.c: **Association is a tendency for one item to bring another to mind, whereas similarity concerns shared properties.** TIGER and STRIPES can be associated without being two similar objects. A list composed entirely of wild animals could also encourage different responses from a list composed of household appliances.
support: Participants may use a deliberate strategy, and the surrounding list can influence which ideas are accessible. Interpreting association norms therefore includes asking how the cue was presented and what other cues were present. These are features of this measurement task itself.
pages.d: A norm is evidence about responses under specified conditions. The distinction between association and similarity matters because an experiment can compare words that are connected in experience without treating them as members of the same category.

pages.title: Neurally inspired concepts in psycholinguistics
pages.c: **Activation, connected representations and learning** provide a vocabulary for explaining language processing. A representation can become active, pass activation to connected representations and become easier to activate through experience. Processing can proceed from sensory features toward words or from word knowledge toward the interpretation of features.
support: A distributed representation encodes an item through a pattern across units. Associative learning changes relationships between units that are active together. These ideas connect the organization of knowledge with the time course of recognizing and producing language.
pages.d: The explanatory goal is to specify what a representation does. Its activity, its connections and the way those connections change determine how input can influence a response.

pages.title: Selective neural activation
pages.c: **A neuron’s response can depend on a particular combination of stimulus features.** In the Hubel and Wiesel example, a simple cell in primary visual cortex responds differently as an oriented line moves through its receptive field. The strongest response occurs for upward movement of a line oriented at about 315 degrees.
support: A receptive field is the part of the sensory input to which the cell responds. Comparing activity across controlled changes in orientation and movement tells us what information is represented by that cell’s response. The cell is sensitive to a combination of properties rather than responding equally to every line.
pages.d: Representation can be inferred from selective response. If a cell consistently responds more to one orientation-and-motion combination, its firing carries information that distinguishes that combination from the alternatives.
pages.visual: Each row pairs an oriented bar and movement arrows with a neural recording. The dense spikes in the preferred condition mark stronger activity. The sparse traces for other conditions show that the response depends on the stimulus features.

pages.title: Activation for a more complex visual pattern
pages.c: **Neural selectivity can concern a complex pattern such as a face viewed from a particular angle.** An inferotemporal cortex neuron responds strongly to near-profile views of a monkey’s face, with much weaker responses to frontal and rear views. Its activity therefore distinguishes different appearances of the same kind of object.
support: The graph plots face angle horizontally and change in firing rate relative to baseline vertically. Responses rise around 80–100 degrees and are near baseline at the ends of the displayed range. Psycholinguistic models extend the idea of activation to perceptual and conceptual representations.
pages.d: A representation’s activation is graded. The same neuron can respond a little to one view and much more to another, so representation does not imply an all-or-none response whenever a face is present.
pages.visual: The face drawings identify the viewing angles used to elicit the spike records. The largest bars and highest points occur for the profile-like views, linking the physical stimulus to the neuron’s response profile.

pages.title: Words as nodes in a lexical network
pages.c: **A lexical node represents a word in a simplified network.** The nodes labeled LION, TIGER and STRIPES stand for three lexical representations that can receive activation from presented words. Treating them as units makes it possible to describe how evidence for one word changes the state of the system.
support: The input display and the lexical nodes are different levels of description. A visible word supplies perceptual evidence, while the node represents the word that the system could recognize from that evidence.
pages.d: The node is a model component with an activation value. It is useful because the model can specify how much activity it receives and how that activity affects recognition.
pages.visual: The ovals label the candidate words. Their links to the display indicate that perceptual input can activate a lexical representation.

pages.title: Recognizing a word across different appearances
pages.c: **Recognizing LION requires treating several visually different inputs as instances of the same word.** Uppercase and lowercase letters, changes in font and changes in size alter the physical display. A lexical representation has to respond across that variation rather than being tied to one exact printed image.
support: This is a lack-of-invariance problem. The linguistic identity remains stable even though the sensory form varies. The LION node summarizes that identity, while the several printed forms illustrate the variation that recognition must accommodate.
pages.d: A word representation groups together inputs that differ physically but count as the same lexical item. Describing a node as responsive to LION therefore implies a mapping from multiple forms to one word identity.
pages.visual: The different spellings in the display vary in case, typeface and size while all instantiate LION. The emphasized lexical oval marks their common word-level destination.

pages.title: Partial evidence produces partial activation
pages.c: **Activation can be partial before a word is identified.** When LION has little contrast against a visual noise mask, the input supplies weak evidence for that word. The lexical node can receive some activation even while recognition remains uncertain.
support: A graded activation value makes intermediate processing states explicit. The system does not have to remain completely inactive until recognition is complete. Its state can change as useful evidence emerges from the noise.
pages.d: Perception can build toward a decision. Weak input raises a candidate’s activity without yet producing enough support for a confident identification.
pages.visual: The faint LION stimulus is difficult to separate from the surrounding noise. The lightly emphasized node represents the partial word-level response to that low-contrast input.

pages.title: Clearer input increases activation
pages.c: **Increasing the clarity of a word increases the evidence available to its lexical representation.** As LION becomes easier to distinguish from the noise, its node becomes more active. Recognition can therefore be modeled as a changing response to the strength of the input.
support: The physical change is an improvement in the relation between the word signal and the noise mask. The computational change is stronger activity for the word representation. Keeping these two changes distinct explains how a manipulation of the display can influence processing.
pages.d: Stronger sensory evidence supports the same word more strongly. The model links stimulus clarity to the graded activity that develops before an identification response.
pages.visual: LION is more visible against the mask, and its oval is more strongly outlined. These are corresponding changes in the input and in the modeled representation.

pages.title: The perceptual identification task
pages.c: **A perceptual identification task measures when a participant can recognize an item.** The participant presses a button as soon as the word becomes identifiable. When the signal-to-noise ratio is sufficiently favorable, LION supplies enough evidence to support recognition and the response can occur.
support: Signal-to-noise ratio describes the strength of the useful word information relative to the interfering background. The response time connects an observable button press with the model’s account of accumulating or increasing activation.
pages.d: The measured outcome is the time required to identify the item. A condition that makes identification easier can shift that response earlier, allowing experimental comparisons of the factors that influence word recognition.
pages.visual: The clear LION display and strongly emphasized LION node illustrate the recognition state. TIGER and STRIPES remain alternative lexical nodes rather than the identified word.

pages.title: Separating stimulus properties from experimental context
pages.c: **Identification speed can depend on both the word being identified and the circumstances in which it appears.** Features of the stimulus itself concern the target item. Features of the experimental environment concern the surrounding experience, including what the participant has just encountered.
support: Separating these sources of influence helps turn a general observation about faster recognition into a testable comparison. The same target can be presented under different contexts, or different targets can be compared under the same task conditions.
pages.d: A recognition task is shaped by more than visibility alone. The properties of the target and the context established by the experiment can each change how quickly the participant identifies it.

pages.title: Frequency, similarity and priming
pages.c: **Word frequency, lexical similarity and recent experience can influence recognition speed.** A word encountered frequently in everyday experience can be easier to activate. Similarity to other words creates neighborhood relationships. Recent exposure to the same word produces repetition priming, while exposure to a related word can produce other forms of priming.
support: Frequency concerns accumulated experience with a word, whereas repetition priming concerns its recent presentation. The distinction matters even though both can make a representation more accessible. A related prime changes the context without repeating the target itself.
pages.d: To explain an identification advantage, ask what differed between conditions. A common target, a recently repeated target and a target preceded by a related word involve different relationships between experience and current processing.

pages.title: Frequency effects and activation dynamics
pages.c: **Activation dynamics describe how a representation’s activity changes over time.** A word’s activation can rise as input supports it and fall after that support ends. Repeated experience with a word can tune the system so that frequently encountered words are easier to activate, providing an account of frequency effects.
support: The CAVE example represents activity at the word level in an interactive activation model. Several candidates can have changing activity while the representation best supported by the input develops the strongest response. A model must specify the mechanism through which experience changes that time course.
pages.d: Frequency is connected to processing through learning. Familiarity affects how readily the system responds to a word, rather than serving as a separate label attached after recognition.
pages.visual: The horizontal dimension is time and the vertical dimension is activation. The large CAVE peak rises above the smaller competing curves, and its gradual decline demonstrates that activation has a time course.

pages.title: Residual activation explains repetition priming
pages.c: **Repetition priming can arise because activation remains elevated after a word has been processed.** Activity does not disappear the moment the input ends. If the same word appears again while some activation remains, its representation begins from a higher level and can reach an identification state more easily.
support: This account relates faster identification to the dynamics of the representation. Activity may increase rapidly and decline more gradually. A short interval between presentations leaves more residual activation available for the second encounter.
pages.d: The first presentation changes the system that receives the second presentation. Residual activation provides a concrete reason that an identical word can be identified more quickly when it is repeated soon afterward.
pages.visual: The falling side of the CAVE curve remains above its earlier baseline. A repetition during that decline starts from an already elevated state rather than from the original resting level.

pages.title: Relationships between lexical representations
pages.c: **Neighborhood effects and related-word priming require relationships among representations.** Similar words can influence one another because they share relevant properties or connections. A prime can also alter the processing of a different target through an associative, semantic or phonological relationship.
support: Repetition concerns the same word on two occasions. Related-word priming instead requires an explanation for how processing one representation changes another. A connected network provides a mechanism for that influence.
pages.d: A model of isolated word nodes could explain changes in the activity of an individual word. Explaining an effect from a different word requires specifying how their representations interact.

pages.title: Connections make a lexical network interactive
pages.c: **Connections allow activity in one lexical node to influence another.** In a network containing LION, TIGER and STRIPES, the nodes are linked rather than functioning as isolated detectors. These links make it possible for the effects of a presented word to extend beyond its own representation.
support: The perceptual input can activate LION directly. A connection between lexical nodes can then carry an influence from LION to TIGER. This separates direct activation from the stimulus and indirect activation through the network.
pages.d: A lexical network describes both representations and relationships. The relationship matters computationally because it changes how one representation responds when another is active.
pages.visual: The links between the ovals add a path across the lexical level. LION and TIGER are connected, and TIGER is linked with STRIPES.

pages.title: Spreading activation and semantic priming
pages.c: **Spreading activation explains how processing one word can prepare the system to process a related word.** Activating LION can send some activity along a weighted connection to TIGER. Connection strengths represent the strength of associations, so different relationships can transmit different amounts of influence.
support: Semantic priming is a behavioral consequence that this network can explain. The target representation is partly activated by the prime, making it more accessible when the target itself appears. Association norms provide one way to characterize which words are related.
pages.d: A prime can change the target’s starting state without being the target. The explanation depends on a path through the network and on the strength of the connections along that path.
pages.visual: The semantic network links items such as vehicle, car and bus, and links fire engine with both vehicles and fire-related concepts. Multiple connections allow one activated concept to influence several related representations.

pages.title: STRIPES in visual noise
pages.c: STRIPES is embedded in a strong noise mask at the start of a perceptual-identification sequence. The low contrast makes the word signal difficult to separate from the background.
pages.d: The target can begin receiving sensory support even when the available evidence is too weak for a confident identification.
pages.visual: The word occupies the center of the noise field and is barely visible at this contrast.

pages.title: Emerging evidence for STRIPES
pages.c: As the contrast of STRIPES increases, more of its letter pattern becomes available against the noise. The physical input now provides stronger support for identifying the same word.
pages.d: Changing clarity changes the evidence for the target without changing the target’s lexical identity.
pages.visual: The central letter sequence is faint but more distinguishable from the mask.

pages.title: Increasing visibility of STRIPES
pages.c: STRIPES becomes increasingly identifiable as its contrast improves. In the perceptual-identification task, the participant responds when the available evidence is sufficient to recognize the word.
pages.d: The demonstration connects stimulus quality with the point at which an identification response becomes possible.
pages.visual: The letters are now visibly separated from the surrounding noise.

pages.title: Recognizable STRIPES
pages.c: The clearer STRIPES stimulus provides stronger word information than the heavily masked versions. A participant who recognizes the word can now make the identification response.
pages.d: The response reflects recognition of the target rather than a judgment about whether stripes are associated with a particular animal.
pages.visual: The word remains within the same type of noise field, while its letter pattern has become clearer.

pages.title: Identifying STRIPES
pages.c: The high-contrast STRIPES display makes the target readily distinguishable from the mask. Recognizing it activates the lexical representation for STRIPES in the network account.
pages.d: The identification event supplies a potential prime. Its effect on another word depends on the connections between their representations.
pages.visual: The dark letter sequence stands out from the gray noise background.

pages.title: LION in visual noise
pages.c: LION is the target in a second perceptual-identification sequence. It begins with weak contrast against a noise mask, so the letter pattern supplies little usable information.
pages.d: The target word and its visibility can be distinguished from its recent context. A priming account asks whether preceding experience changes how quickly this target can be recognized.
pages.visual: The short word is centered in the noise field and is initially difficult to read.

pages.title: Emerging evidence for LION
pages.c: Increasing the contrast of LION strengthens the perceptual evidence for that word. Recognition becomes more likely as the letter pattern separates from the background noise.
pages.d: The same target can produce a changing internal response because the quality of its sensory evidence changes.
pages.visual: LION is faintly visible in the center of the mask.

pages.title: Increasing visibility of LION
pages.c: LION becomes clearer within the mask. A perceptual-identification response can occur when this evidence supports recognizing the target, and the time of that response is the measurable outcome.
pages.d: A priming comparison concerns whether recognition occurs sooner under one preceding context than another. The visible target supplies the common object of that comparison.
pages.visual: The four letters have greater contrast than in the more strongly masked display.

pages.title: Recognizable LION
pages.c: The more visible LION stimulus supplies substantial evidence for its lexical identity. The network explanation links that evidence with increasing activation of the LION representation.
pages.d: The clarity of the target and any activation left by its context can jointly contribute to the state from which recognition occurs.
pages.visual: The word is legible while the surrounding noise mask remains present.

pages.title: Identifying LION
pages.c: The clear LION stimulus completes the identification sequence. Its lexical node can be activated directly by the word input and can also be influenced through connections with other nodes.
pages.d: The distinction between direct input and activity arriving through the network is central to explaining mediated priming.
pages.visual: The strong word signal is easily distinguishable from the noise field.

pages.title: Mediated priming through TIGER
pages.c: **Mediated priming occurs when a prime influences a target through an intermediate representation.** STRIPES can activate TIGER, and TIGER can pass activation to LION. STRIPES and LION can therefore influence one another even when they lack a direct associative connection.
support: The intermediate node supplies a route that a direct-association account would miss. Recognizing STRIPES raises activity elsewhere in the network, making LION more accessible through TIGER. This is why an effect between indirectly connected words supports spreading activation.
pages.d: The crucial relationship is the chain. STRIPES is connected to TIGER and TIGER is connected to LION, so the influence can travel beyond the prime’s immediate neighbor.
pages.visual: The bold STRIPES oval marks the presented prime, while TIGER occupies the middle of the chain. LION has no drawn direct connection to STRIPES. Its influence arrives by way of TIGER.

pages.title: A small effect can distinguish processing accounts
pages.c: **An unexpected priming effect can reveal the organization of a processing system.** STRIPES and LION are not obvious direct associates, yet an effect between them makes sense if activity travels through a shared connection with TIGER. Careful experimental design allows such a small effect to bear on a specific account of lexical organization.
support: The theoretical value comes from the relationship being tested, not simply from the size of the difference. A mediated relationship predicts an influence that would be unexplained by a model restricted to direct associations.
pages.d: A useful experiment makes alternative explanations predict different outcomes. The indirect STRIPES–TIGER–LION path turns a counterintuitive observation into evidence about how activity moves through representations.

pages.title: Bottom-up evidence and top-down word support
pages.c: **Bottom-up processing carries information from visual features toward letters and words, while top-down processing lets word knowledge influence letter interpretation.** In an interactive activation model, partially visible features support candidate letters and words. A strongly supported word can then feed activation back to the letters that fit it, helping complete a noisy pattern.
support: For the masked WORK example, word-level support favors the final K. The network contains candidate words such as WORK, WORD, WEAR and WERK, allowing letter evidence and word-level evidence to interact over time. The alternatives do not have to remain equally plausible as processing continues.
pages.d: Pattern completion follows from reciprocal influence. Sensory evidence constrains which words become active, and an active word supports its compatible letters. The model can therefore strengthen an interpretation of an ambiguous letter through the larger pattern in which it occurs.
pages.visual: Features occupy the bottom of the network, letters the middle and words the top. In the output graph, the K curve rises strongly while the R and D alternatives remain low. This supports K as the final letter of WORK.

pages.title: Associative learning changes connection strength
pages.c: **Hebbian learning links repeated coactivation with stronger connections.** The phrase “neurons that fire together, wire together” captures the idea that activity occurring together can change how strongly one unit influences another. Learning therefore changes the network that will process future input.
support: The bell-and-food example connects a bell signal and a food signal with a salivation pathway. When the relevant units are active together, the bell connection to the response pathway is strengthened. An initially weak influence can become more effective through that experience.
pages.d: Associative learning explains a change in processing through a change in connection strength. In language research, an important question is how much structure such mechanisms can learn and how their operation may interact with prior constraints.
pages.visual: The arrow labeled “synapse to be strengthened” identifies the bell input to the salivation-related unit. The food detector supplies another input to that response pathway, making their joint activation the relevant learning event.

pages.title: Distributed representations support generalization
pages.c: **A distributed representation encodes an item through a pattern across multiple units.** Similar items can have overlapping patterns, allowing knowledge acquired about one item to influence another. An associative model can then generalize properties learned about robins and canaries to new birds because it represents their similarity.
support: The network combines an item input with a relation input and produces an attribute output. A request about what a canary can do activates a different kind of relation from a request about what it is. Shared internal representations allow information about related items to contribute to these responses.
pages.d: Generalization depends on the way knowledge is represented. If related examples share internal structure, learning from one example changes part of the machinery used for another. A model can then produce an appropriate response to a combination it has not simply memorized as an isolated pair.
pages.visual: The selected item is canary and the selected relation is can. Active output attributes include grow, move, fly and sing. The representation and hidden layers connect the item–relation combination with that distributed set of properties.

pages.title: Connecting activation, learning and representation
pages.c: **A network account links the current activity of representations with the experience that shaped their connections.** Activation changes as input is processed. Spreading activation allows one representation to influence another. Associative learning changes connection strengths, while distributed representations provide a basis for similarity and generalization.
support: Bottom-up and top-down processing describe directions of influence between levels. Priming experiments help investigate this organization by measuring how processing one item changes the processing of another. Together these concepts connect representations, mechanisms and observable behavior.
pages.d: The same framework can address several questions. What becomes active concerns representation, how activity spreads concerns connectivity, and how experience changes future responses concerns learning.

questions.stem: Why does TIGER–STRIPES illustrate association without similarity?
choices: One names an animal and the other a property linked to that animal.
Both name animals in the same biological category.
Their spelling differs, so they cannot be semantically connected.
STRIPES is the plural of TIGER.
questions.why: Association concerns a connection that makes one item bring another to mind. Similarity concerns shared properties or category membership.

questions.stem: What supports interpreting the V1 cell as selective for a combination of features?
choices: Its firing changes systematically with line orientation and direction of movement.
It responds identically whenever any visible object is present.
It has a receptive field that includes every location in the visual world.
Its strongest response is produced after the participant names the line.
questions.why: Controlled changes in the line reveal selective responses to orientation and movement within the receptive field.

questions.stem: What recognition problem is illustrated by LION in different fonts and cases?
choices: The same lexical identity must be recovered from physically varying inputs.
Each typeface must have a different word meaning.
The noise mask must contain a different animal name each time.
A lexical node can respond only after the font has been named aloud.
questions.why: The lack-of-invariance problem concerns stable linguistic identity despite variation in the sensory input.

questions.stem: What is measured in the perceptual identification task described here?
choices: When a participant can identify the item and makes the response.
How many dictionary definitions the participant can generate.
How strongly the participant likes the displayed word.
Which animal has the clearest stripes.
questions.why: Participants respond when the masked word becomes identifiable. Response timing allows conditions affecting recognition to be compared.

questions.stem: How can an activation account explain a word-frequency advantage?
choices: Experience tunes the system so frequent words are easier to activate.
Frequent words are always displayed with a larger font.
Frequent words have no neighboring lexical representations.
The target is identified before any activity changes over time.
questions.why: Frequency concerns accumulated experience, which can change the dynamics through which a representation becomes active.

questions.stem: Why can repeating a word soon after its first presentation speed identification?
choices: Some activation remains, so the repeated word starts from an elevated state.
Its lexical representation has been permanently removed from competition.
Its meaning becomes unrelated to its form after one presentation.
The visual noise disappears from every repeated trial.
questions.why: Residual activation links the recent presentation to an easier starting state for subsequent processing of the same word.

questions.stem: What does a weighted connection add to a spreading-activation account?
choices: Related representations can influence one another by different strengths.
Every representation must have exactly the same activation.
Only identical words can be connected.
It prevents a prime from changing a target representation.
questions.why: Weights specify how strongly activity in one representation affects another, allowing association strength to matter.

questions.stem: What makes STRIPES priming LION a case of mediated priming?
choices: Their influence can pass through their connections with TIGER.
STRIPES and LION are two visual versions of the same word.
The participant must say TIGER aloud before recognizing LION.
The two words are assumed to have identical meanings.
questions.why: A mediating node supplies an indirect path from the prime to the target without requiring a direct STRIPES–LION connection.

questions.stem: Which influence is top-down in the interactive activation example?
choices: An activated word supports a compatible interpretation of an ambiguous letter.
A line feature provides evidence for a letter.
Improved contrast makes a letter’s physical edges clearer.
A visual input first reaches the feature detectors.
questions.why: Top-down influence travels from a higher-level word representation toward letter interpretation. Feature-to-letter influence is bottom-up.

questions.stem: Why are overlapping distributed representations useful for generalization?
choices: Learning about one item can affect shared structure used to represent related items.
Each new item must receive a wholly unrelated pattern with no shared units.
The model can replace all learned attributes with a single item label.
Similarity becomes irrelevant once a network contains connections.
questions.why: Overlap represents similarity, allowing learned properties of familiar birds to support responses about related or newly encountered birds.

written.prompt: Explain how STRIPES can facilitate identification of LION in a spreading-activation account.
answer: STRIPES activates TIGER through an associative connection. TIGER is connected to LION, so some activation can reach LION indirectly.
This mediated route prepares the LION representation without requiring STRIPES and LION to be direct associates.

written.prompt: Distinguish a frequency effect from repetition priming using activation dynamics.
answer: A frequency effect reflects accumulated experience that makes a commonly encountered word easier to activate.
Repetition priming reflects recent processing of the same word. Residual activation can remain elevated when the repeated input arrives.

guide.title: Association norms and stable lexical identity

experiments.title: Hubel and Wiesel · selective visual responses
